short: Calderón's problem from one boundary patch

title.title: Calderón's problem from one boundary patch
title.subtitle: Claim: boundary data on one patch determine a smooth metric in dimension $n \ge 3$; rough conductivities can fool it

plain: Measure voltages and currents on one small patch of a body's skin: can you tell what is inside?

beats.text: Calderón (1980): do voltage-to-current measurements at the boundary determine the inside?
Claimed: a smooth metric is fixed by data on one patch $\Gamma$, in dimension $n \ge 3$
Formalized instead: two rough conductivities in $\mathbb R^3$ with identical data

steps: Match harmonic coordinates near the measured patch
Extend the match outward, across one surface at a time
Shrinking-sphere estimates carry it through the whole body

achievement.label: Lee–Uhlmann conjecture (1989), with same-patch partial data
statement: n \ge 3: \ \ \Lambda_g \text{ on } \Gamma \;\Rightarrow\; g \text{ up to a diffeomorphism fixing } \Gamma
achievement.context: Before: the real-analytic case; smooth isotropic conductivities by Sylvester–Uhlmann (1987)
achievement.note: High-risk: the smooth uniqueness papers have no Lean and need expert review

verify.detail: Lean: only the $L^\infty$ nonuniqueness in $\mathbb R^3$, about 75k lines. Smooth uniqueness is paper only
verify.ourCheck: We compared the Lean scope with the papers; we did not build it

voice.text: Do boundary measurements determine the inside? Claimed: data on one patch fix a smooth metric.
Match coordinates at the patch, then extend outward surface by surface.
Claimed: one patch suffices, dimension three up.
